title: [New Rx] Pax Silica: Street protesters vs boardroom promoters. But where’s the beef?
summary: The Philippines is overlooking a more fundamental question: Why would global technology companies choose to invest here over other Asian economies?

blocks.text: The Philippines has a remarkable ability to turn an economic development proposal into a national controversy before a single factory has been built. The latest example is Pax Silica, the United States-led initiative to strengthen supply chains for semiconductors, artificial intelligence, critical minerals, and advanced manufacturing.

Supporters have celebrated its potential to bring billions of dollars in investment. Protesters have organized demonstrations against American influence, environmental risks, and displacement of Indigenous communities. Some demonstrations have led to confrontations with authorities and traffic disruptions across Metro Manila.

I respect the right to peaceful protest, but are the arguments proportionate to what has actually been agreed upon? We are spending enormous energy debating investments that have not yet materialized, as though American companies are already lining up to build factories here.
Perhaps both supporters and protesters are overlooking a more fundamental question: What makes the Philippines attractive enough for these investments in the first place?

I frequently travel to Taiwan, South Korea, Singapore, and other Asian markets. One thing surprises me: very few businesspeople I meet seem familiar with Pax Silica. These are countries with sophisticated technology industries where executives discuss actual capital expenditures, manufacturing capacity, and investment transactions.

South Korea, Japan, and Singapore were among Pax Silica’s original signatories in December 2025; the Philippines joined in April 2026. Yet, much of the excitement seems concentrated in Manila. Perhaps these other countries do not need a diplomatic initiative to validate their attractiveness to investors because they already possess established industrial ecosystems.

In April, Washington and Manila announced plans for a 1,620-hectare Economic Security Zone in New Clark City, with projections of $40 billion to $70 billion in investments. But projections are not commitments. After months of enthusiastic announcements, US Ambassador Lee Lipton clarified in November that no agreement signing had ever been planned for the ASEAN Summit.

The Department of Trade and Industry maintained that negotiations were progressing, but the episode illustrates how easily expectations can get ahead of commitments. Diplomatic support, a signed framework, and actual investment are three very different things, and the government should be careful about presenting projected investments as secured achievements.

There is a tendency in Manila to amplify statements from business promoters as though they represent Washington’s intentions. Commercial enthusiasm should not automatically become the basis for national economic expectations. Politicians and intermediaries have incentives to promote ambitious figures, but projected investments should never substitute for measurable economic accomplishments. We must stop confusing access with influence, influence with policy, and policy with investment.

We tend to view American economic engagement exclusively through a US-Philippines lens. But Washington has similar conversations throughout Asia — with South Korea, Taiwan, Japan, Singapore, India, Malaysia, Thailand, Vietnam, and Indonesia — often with countries possessing far more developed industrial capabilities. What appears to be a major breakthrough through a US-Philippines lens may be just one of many initiatives considered from Washington’s perspective.

Supporters point to our mineral wealth, but consider nickel: the Philippines produced 330,000 metric tons in 2024 compared to Indonesia’s 2.2 million metric tons, and Indonesia processes its nickel locally while we mostly export raw ore.

Investors need commercially viable processing facilities, competitive electricity, and reliable infrastructure. Having land does not automatically make us an attractive data center destination, having nickel does not make us competitive in processing, and having an American ally does not automatically make us an advanced industrial economy.

If Pax Silica is supposed to transform our technology economy, where are the binding commitments from major semiconductor manufacturers and AI providers? An industrial zone does not become an AI ecosystem simply because officials put artificial intelligence on a presentation. I would be more impressed by a confirmed $500 million investment from a credible manufacturer than another announcement celebrating a potential $70 billion development.

blocks.text: Protesters should continue demanding safeguards peacefully, business promoters should distinguish commercial aspirations from binding commitments, and government officials should stop letting public expectations run ahead of reality. The Philippines should focus on affordable electricity, reliable infrastructure, faster permitting, technical education, and predictable regulation.

We already participate in semiconductor assembly, testing, and packaging, which offers a realistic pathway toward higher-value manufacturing. Furthermore, Asian suppliers from Taiwan, Korea, or Japan could deliver greater immediate economic benefits than an ambitious American initiative that takes decades to materialize.

I am not opposed to Pax Silica if it brings productive investment under appropriate safeguards. But the Philippines should not become so preoccupied with symbolic engagement that it neglects the fundamentals of economic competitiveness. The question is not whether America will choose the Philippines for Pax Silica, but whether the Philippines can become a country where global investors actually want to invest even without it. – Rappler.com

Dr. Jaemin Park is a physician, healthcare investor, and adjunct professor at UP Manila College of Public Health. He writes about healthcare economics, investment, and public policy in the Philippines and across Asia.
